questions.q: The two main forms of cell death are:

options.e: Correct. These are the two major forms.
Wrong. Regeneration is repair, not death.

questions.q: Which feature best defines necrosis?

options.t: Change of one adult cell type to another
Cells rupture and release contents, causing local inflammation
options.e: Correct. Loss of membrane integrity leads to leakage and inflammation.

questions.q: Which sequence of nuclear changes occurs in necrosis?

options.e: Correct. Shrinkage, then fragmentation, then dissolution.
Wrong. Karyolysis is the last step.

questions.q: Pyknosis is:

options.e: Correct. DNA condenses into a solid shrunken mass.

questions.q: Why do necrotic cells appear more eosinophilic?

options.t: Increased binding of eosin to denatured cytoplasmic proteins
options.e: Correct. Denatured proteins take up more eosin.
Wrong. Lipid is washed out as clear space.

questions.q: Which pattern of necrosis is characteristic of ischemia in solid organs such as heart and kidney?

options.e: Wrong. Typical of infection and brain infarcts.
Correct. Preserved tissue outlines with loss of nuclei, called infarction.

questions.q: Cerebral infarction produces which type of necrosis?

options.e: Wrong. This is typical of solid organs such as the heart and kidney.
Wrong. Seen in vessel walls in immune reactions.
Correct. The brain liquefies even when sterile.

questions.q: A lung biopsy shows granulomas with cheesy, amorphous granular pink centres. This is:

options.e: Correct. Characteristic of tuberculosis and some fungal infections.
Wrong. A clinical term for limb necrosis.

questions.q: Which infection typically produces caseous necrosis?

options.e: Correct. Mycobacterial infection gives cheese-like necrosis.

options.t: Urinary tract infection by E. coli
options.e: Wrong. Usually gives suppuration, not caseation.

questions.q: Chalky white lesions in the peritoneum of a patient with acute pancreatitis are due to:

options.t: Fat saponification by calcium combining with fatty acids
options.e: Correct. Released lipases digest fat, and fatty acids bind calcium.

questions.q: Fat necrosis microscopically shows:

options.t: Preserved outlines of eosinophilic cells with no nuclei
Pink amorphous material in vessel walls
Shadowy outlines of fat cells surrounded by basophilic calcium

questions.q: Traumatic fat necrosis is classically seen in which organ?

options.e: Correct. Trauma to the breast fat causes it.

questions.q: What is the difference between dry and wet gangrene?

options.t: Dry stays intact; wet liquefies after bacterial infection
Dry is caused by infection, wet by ischemia
options.e: Wrong. Both arise from ischemia; infection makes it wet.

options.t: Dry occurs in the brain, wet in the limbs
options.e: Wrong. Gangrene typically applies to limbs.
Wrong. They differ in appearance and infection.

questions.q: Fibrinoid necrosis is most commonly seen in:

options.e: Correct. Immune complexes and plasma proteins deposit in vessel walls.

questions.q: Which serum marker is used to diagnose myocardial infarction?

options.e: Correct. It leaks from damaged cardiac cells.

questions.q: Raised amylase and lipase indicate necrosis of which organ?

options.e: Wrong. Troponin is used for the heart.
Correct. These pancreatic enzymes leak after injury.
Wrong. AST and ALT are used for the liver.

questions.q: Apoptosis is best described as:

options.t: Programmed cell death without harmful inflammation
Replacement of one cell type by another

questions.q: Which enzymes drive apoptosis?

options.e: Wrong. Involved in membrane injury by calcium.
Correct. Their activation leads to nuclease and protease activity.

questions.q: Which are the two pathways of caspase activation?

options.e: Wrong. These are patterns of necrosis.
Correct. These are the two recognized pathways.
